newsitem.title: GERMANY: Sick pay proposal unviable--German metal employers.
newsitem.headline: Sick pay proposal unviable--German metal employers.

text.p: German metal and engineering employers said on Tuesday they had come close to agreeing a new deal on sick payments with workers but backed out in the end because they believed the scheme would have proved unworkable.

Union officials had warned on Monday that any failure to find agreement on sick pay costs, which employers are determined to cut, would make strikes in the sector early next year all the Speaking after the collapse of talks with the IG Metall trade union in the state of North-Rhine Westphalia, employers' negotiator Martin Kannegiesser said a deal under which sick pay could be offset by cuts in other bonuses had been proposed.

"We discussed this idea at length but concluded that it contained so many problems, incalculables and inequalities that applying it would have resulted in disputes and differing interpretations," Kannegiesser told German radio.
Any agreement in the key steel-making region of North-Rhine Westphalia could then have been proposed as a "pilot agreement" on a national level.

Now the dispute on sick pay, which was triggered by a new law in October allowing employers to cut payments from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, is likely to be included in the regular 1997 wage round, due to start early next year.
Walter Riester, deputy chairman of IG Metall, had said on Monday that if no agreement was reached then, a strike ballot could be called by the end of February.
"Then I am sure we will end up striking," he said on German radio.
The collapse of the talks came even though the two sides had agreed over a wage increase of 1.5 percent next year and 2.5 percent in 1998 for the 850,000 metal and engineering workers in the region.
Previous attempts to solve the row had focused on a proposals by employers to maintain sick pay at 100 percent but deduct holiday time from workers in the case of long-term illness.

According to Kannegiesser, the new scheme proposed in North-Rhine Westphalia would have linked Christmas bonuses to the absenteeism in a particular company, with low absenteeism rewarded by high end-of-year bonuses.
Kannegiesser said that while employer negiotators had originally thought such a model could offer them the cost savings they are seeking, the ultimately rejected it as unworkable.

Overall, metal and engineering employers are seeking a 1997 wage deal that would leave overall labour costs in the sector unchanged. Union leaders are meanwhile aiming to secure agreements protecting jobs in the sector.
